column2: Book One: on the nature of civilization in creation and what occurs in it of Bedouin life and settled life, domination, earning, livelihood, the crafts, the sciences and the like, and the causes and reasons behind these

Know that, since the reality of history is that it is a report about human social organization, which is the civilization of the world, and about the conditions that befall the nature of that civilization, such as savagery and sociability, group solidarities (ʿaṣabiyyāt), the various kinds of domination of human beings over one another, and the royal authority and dynasties and their ranks that arise from that, and what human beings take up through their works and endeavors of earning, livelihood, the sciences and the crafts, and all the other conditions that arise from that civilization by its nature; and since falsehood by its nature finds its way into reports, and has causes that bring it about, among these causes are partisanships for opinions and schools of thought. For the soul, when it is in a state of balance in accepting a report, gives it its due of scrutiny and examination until it can tell its truth from its falsehood; but if partisanship for an opinion or a creed possesses it, it accepts at first glance whatever reports agree with it, and that inclination and partisanship become a covering over the eye of its insight, keeping it from criticism and scrutiny, so that it falls into accepting falsehood and passing it on. Another of the causes that bring about falsehood in reports is trust in the transmitters, and the scrutiny of that goes back to authentication and impugnment (taʿdīl and jarḥ). Another is heedlessness of intentions: many transmitters do not know the intention behind what they witnessed or heard, and relate the report according to their own supposition and conjecture, and so fall into falsehood.

Another is imagining [a report] to be true, which is frequent and for the most part comes from trusting the transmitters. Another is ignorance of how to fit conditions to the events, because of the deception and artifice that enter into them, so that the reporter relates them as he saw them, though through artifice they are in themselves other than the truth. Another is that people, for the most part, curry favor with those who hold esteem and rank by praise and eulogy, by making their conditions look good and spreading their renown through that, so that reports of them become widespread though untrue; for souls are fond of being praised, and people look eagerly to this world and its means, whether standing or wealth, and for the most part they do not aspire to virtues or compete with those who possess them. Another of the causes that bring it about, and one that comes before all those mentioned, is ignorance of the natures of conditions in civilization. For every event, whether an entity or an act, must have a nature peculiar to it, in itself and in the conditions that befall it; so if the hearer knows the natures of events and conditions in existence and what they require, that helps him, in scrutinizing a report, to tell truth from falsehood, and this is more effective in scrutiny than any other approach that may present itself. Hearers very often come to accept impossible reports and pass them on, and they are handed down from them, as al-Masʿūdī related about Alexander when the beasts of the sea kept him from building Alexandria

and how he made a glass chest and dived in it to the bottom of the sea until he portrayed those demonic beasts that he saw, and made figures of them out of metal bodies and set them up facing the building; and those beasts, when they came out and saw them, fled, and the building of the city was completed — in a long story made up of impossible fables. It is impossible because of his making the glass casket and meeting the sea and its waves with his own body; and because kings do not bring themselves to such recklessness, and whoever among them undertakes it has exposed himself to destruction, to the breaking of the bond [of allegiance] and to the gathering of the people around someone else, and in that is his ruin, and they would not wait for his return from that recklessness of his for so much as the blink of an eye; and because the jinn are not known to have forms or figures peculiar to them, but are only able to take on shapes, and as for the many heads that are said to belong to them, what is meant by it is only hideousness and terror, not that it is real.

And all of these discredit that story, but what discredits it and shows it to be impossible from the standpoint of natural reality is plainer than all of this: a person immersed in water, even if he were inside the chest, would find the air too confined for natural breathing, and his spirit would quickly grow hot because of how little there is, so that he would lose the cold air that tempers the constitution of the lung and the spirit of the heart, and would die on the spot. This is the reason for the death of people in bathhouses when these are sealed against the cold air, and of those lowered into wells and deep-shafted pits when the air in them has been heated by putrefaction and no winds enter to stir it; the person lowered into them dies at once. And this is the cause of the death of the fish when it leaves the sea: the air is not enough to temper its lung, since that is excessively hot, and the water that tempers it is cold, while the air it has come out into is hot, so the heat overpowers its animal spirit and it dies all at once. From this, too, comes the death of those struck by lightning, and the like. Among impossible reports also is what al-Masʿūdī relates about the figure of the starling that is in Rome: on a known day of the year starlings gather to it carrying olives, and from this they make their oil. And see how far that is from the natural course in the making of oil.

Another is what al-Bakrī relates about the building of the city called Dhāt al-Abwāb, whose circuit extends over more than thirty stages and which has 10,000 gates. Cities are built only for protection and refuge, as will be explained, and this one went beyond what could be encompassed, so that it would have neither stronghold nor refuge. And likewise what al-Masʿūdī also relates in the story of the City of Brass: that it is a city all of whose construction is brass, in the desert of Sijilmāsa; that Mūsā ibn Nuṣayr came upon it in his campaign into the Maghrib; that its gates are shut; and that whoever climbs up to it by its walls, when he looks over the wall, claps his hands and throws himself down, and does not return until the end of time — a story impossible in the ordinary course of things, from the fables of storytellers. The desert of Sijilmāsa has been combed by riders and guides, and they have found no report of this city. Moreover, all these conditions that they mention of it are impossible in the ordinary course of things and contrary to natural matters in the building and laying out of cities; and as for metals, the most that exists of them is that they are used for vessels and household goods, while the erecting of a city out of them is, as you can see, impossible and remote. Things like this are many, and scrutinizing them is done only by knowing the natures of civilization. That is the best and most reliable method of scrutinizing reports and telling their truth from their falsehood, and it comes before scrutiny by the authentication of transmitters, and one does not turn to the authentication of transmitters until it is known that the report is in itself possible or impossible

but if it is impossible, there is no use in examining authentication and impugnment. Indeed, the people of rational inquiry have counted among the grounds for attacking a report the impossibility of what its wording signifies, or of its interpretation in a way that reason does not accept. Authentication and impugnment are what is taken into account for the soundness of reports of the sharia only because most of them are enacted religious obligations (takālīf) that the Lawgiver has made it binding to act on, provided that a probable belief in their truth has been reached, and the way to the soundness of that belief is trust in the transmitters on the grounds of probity and accuracy. But reports about events require, for their truth and soundness, that conformity [with reality] be taken into account; therefore one must examine whether it is possible for the event to occur, and this, in their case, became more important than authentication and takes precedence over it, since the benefit of an enactment is derived from authentication alone, whereas the benefit of a report is derived from it and from external reality through conformity. That being so, the rule for telling the true from the false in reports by means of possibility and impossibility is that we examine human social organization, which is civilization, and distinguish what befalls it essentially and by the requirement of its nature from what is accidental and not to be reckoned with, and from what cannot possibly befall it. And when

we have done that, this will be for us a rule for telling the true from the false in reports, and truth from falsehood, in a demonstrative way into which doubt has no entry. Then, when we hear of any of the conditions that have occurred in civilization, we shall know what we judge fit to accept and what we judge to be spurious; and that will be for us a sound standard by which historians seek the path of truth and correctness in what they relate. This is the aim of this first book of our work. And it is as though this were a science standing by itself, for it has a subject, which is human civilization and human social organization, and it has problems, which are the explanation, one after another, of the accidents and conditions that attach to it essentially. This is the way of every science, whether conventional or rational.

Know that discourse on this subject is new in its craft, strange in its tendency and rare in its benefit; inquiry brought us upon it and deep diving led to it. It is not part of the science of rhetoric, which consists only of persuasive and useful statements for winning the general public over to an opinion or turning them away from it; nor is it part of the science of civic politics, since civic politics is the management of the household or the city as ethics and wisdom require, so as to lead the public along a path in which lies the preservation of the species and its survival. Its subject therefore differs from the subject of these two arts, which perhaps resemble it. It is as though it were a science of newly derived origin. Indeed, upon my life, I have not come across discourse in its vein by anyone in creation. I do not know whether that was because of their heedlessness of it, though that is not what one supposes of them, or perhaps they wrote on this subject and treated it exhaustively, and it has not reached us — for the sciences are many, more than those that have reached us. Where are the sciences of the Persians, which ʿUmar, may God be pleased with him, ordered to be erased at the conquest? Where are the sciences of the Chaldeans, the Syriacs and the people of Babylon, and what appeared among them of their traces and results? And where are the sciences of the Copts and of those before them? Only the sciences of one nation have reached us, the Greeks in particular, because of al-Maʾmūn’s passion for bringing them out of their language and his ability to do so through the many translators and the money he spent on them

and we have not come across anything of the sciences of others. If every reality that is by nature an object of thought is fit to be investigated for the accidents that befall it essentially, then for every concept and reality there ought to be a science of its own. But the philosophers perhaps only paid regard in this matter to concern for the fruits [of a science], and the fruit of this one lies only in reports, as you have seen. Although its problems are noble in themselves and in their distinctness, its fruit is the validation of reports, and that is slight; for this reason they abandoned it. God knows best. “And you have been given only a little knowledge” (17: 85). As for this art, which it has occurred to us to examine, we find some of its problems coming up incidentally for the people of the sciences in the proofs of their sciences, and they are of the same kind as its problems in subject and in what is sought: for instance, what the philosophers and scholars mention in proving prophecy, that human beings cooperate in their existence and therefore need in it a ruler and a restraining authority; and what is mentioned in the principles of jurisprudence, in the chapter on establishing languages, that people need to express their purposes by the nature of cooperation and social organization, and that making things plain through verbal expressions is easier; and what the jurists mention in explaining legal rulings by their purposes, that illicit sexual intercourse confuses lineages and corrupts the species, and that killing also corrupts the species

and that injustice portends the ruin of civilization, which leads to the corruption of the species, and the rest of the purposes of the sharia in its rulings, all of which are built on the preservation of civilization, so that they involve consideration of what befalls it; and this is evident from this discussion of ours of these problems cited as examples. Likewise, a few of its problems come down to us in scattered sayings of the sages of creation, but they did not treat it exhaustively. Among them are the words of the Mūbadhān [to] Bahrām ibn Bahrām in the tale of the owls that al-Masʿūdī relates: “O king, royal authority attains its full might only through the sharia, through standing up for God in obedience to Him and acting under His command and prohibition. There is no support for the sharia except through royal authority, no might for royal authority except through men, no support for men except through wealth, no way to wealth except through cultivation, and no way to cultivation except through justice. And justice is the scale set up among creation; the Lord set it up and appointed a guardian over it, who is the king.” And among the words of Anūshirwān to this very effect: “Royal authority is through the army, and the army through wealth, and wealth through the land tax, and the land tax through cultivation, and cultivation through justice, and justice through the reform of the officials, and the reform of the officials through the uprightness of the viziers; and the head of it all is the king’s looking into the condition of his subjects in person and his ability to discipline them, so that he rules them and they do not rule him.”

In the book attributed to Aristotle on politics, which circulates among people, there is a good part of it, but it is not exhaustive, does not give it its due of proofs, and is mixed with other matter. And in that book he alluded to these sayings that we have transmitted from the Mūbadhān and Anūshirwān, and put them in the near circle, the greatest statement about which is his saying: “The world is a garden whose fence is the dynasty. The dynasty is a sovereignty through which the law lives. The law is a policy that royal authority administers. Royal authority is an order that the army supports. The army are helpers whom wealth sustains. Wealth is sustenance that the subjects gather. The subjects are servants whom justice shelters. Justice is a familiar thing, and through it the world stands. The world is a garden.” Then it returns to the beginning of the discourse. So these are eight sayings of wisdom concerning politics, linked one to another, their endings turning back to their beginnings, and joined in a circle whose end cannot be determined; he was proud of having come upon them and made much of their benefits.

And if you consider our discussion in the chapter on dynasties and royal authority and give it its due of perusal and understanding, you will come upon, in the course of it, the explanation of these sayings and the detailing of their general statement, fully and clearly given, with the most comprehensive exposition and the plainest evidence and proof, to which God gave us insight without any instruction from Aristotle or any benefit from a Mūbadhān. Likewise you will find in the words of Ibn al-Muqaffaʿ and in what he goes into by digression in his epistles about politics many of the problems of this book of ours, though not demonstrated as we have demonstrated them; he only sets them forth in the manner of rhetoric, in the style of epistolary writing and eloquence of speech. Likewise the judge Abū Bakr al-Ṭurṭūshī circled around [this subject] in his book Sirāj al-mulūk (“The Lamp of Kings”) and arranged it in chapters close to the chapters and problems of this book of ours, but he did not hit the quarry in it, nor strike the flank, nor treat the problems exhaustively, nor make the proofs clear. He only sets up a chapter for a problem, then piles up many hadiths and traditions, and relates scattered sayings of the sages of the Persians, such as Buzurjmihr and the Mūbadhān, and of the sages of India, and what is handed down from Daniel and Hermes and other great ones of creation. He does not lift a veil from the truth, nor raise a curtain with natural proofs; it is only transmission and compilation resembling sermons. It is as though he hovered around the aim and did not find it, did not realize his purpose and did not treat its problems exhaustively. But we were inspired by God to it by inspiration, and He led us to come upon a science that placed us between the unknown (nakira)

and Juhayna, [who has] the report of it. If I have treated its problems exhaustively and distinguished its inquiries and aspects from all the other crafts, that is success and guidance from God; and if anything has escaped me in enumerating it, or been confused with something else, it is for the critical examiner to put it right, and mine is the credit, for I opened the way for him and made the road clear. God guides by His light whom He wills. We shall now set out in this book what befalls human beings in their social organization of the conditions of civilization, in royal authority, earning, the sciences and the crafts, by demonstrative methods through which the truth becomes clear in the knowledge of the elite and the common people, and by which illusions are dispelled and doubts removed. We say: since the human being is distinguished from all other animals by properties peculiar to him, among them are the sciences and crafts, which are the result of the thought by which he is distinguished from the animals and ennobled, by virtue of that attribute, over the creatures; and among them is the need for a restraining rule and a sovereign power, since among all animals his existence is not possible without that, except what is said about bees and locusts, and these, even if they have something of the kind, have it by way of inspiration, not by thought and deliberation; and among them is striving for livelihood and exerting oneself to obtain it by all its avenues and to acquire its means, because God has made him in need of food for his life and survival and has guided him to seek and pursue it. The Exalted said:

“He gave everything its created form, then guided it” (20: 50). And among them is civilization, which is living together and settling together in a city or an encampment, for companionship with kin and the meeting of needs, because of the disposition in their natures to cooperate in earning a living, as we shall explain. Of this civilization, some is Bedouin, which is in the outlying districts and in the mountains and in the encampments that move in search of pasture in the wastelands and the edges of the sands; and some is settled, which is in the cities, villages, towns and mud-brick settlements, for refuge in them and protection by their walls. In all of these conditions there are matters that befall it, from the standpoint of social organization, as essential accidents of it; so the discussion in this book is necessarily confined to six chapters. The first: on human civilization in general, its kinds, and its share of the earth.

The second: on Bedouin civilization, with mention of the tribes and the savage nations. The third: on dynasties, the caliphate and royal authority, with mention of the sovereign ranks. The fourth: on settled civilization, the towns and the cities. The fifth: on the crafts, livelihood and earning, and its forms. The sixth: on the sciences and their acquisition and learning. I put Bedouin civilization first because it precedes all of them, as we shall show you later; likewise the putting of royal authority before the towns and cities. As for putting livelihood first, it is because livelihood is necessary and natural, while the learning of knowledge is a refinement or a convenience, and the natural comes before the refinement. And I put the crafts with earning because they are in some respects part of it, and from the standpoint of civilization, as we shall show you later. God is the One who grants success to what is right and helps toward it.
